351,765 patients equally distributed across all five age groups — gender balanced throughout

Understanding the demographic foundation of our patient population is the first analytical step — and the most critical correction in this portfolio. Previous analysis reported 85.5% of patients as elderly, leading to misaligned strategy recommendations. Exercise 3 confirms a balanced, general-service population that demands equal investment across all age groups, service lines, and care pathways.

Strategic Implication — General Service Hospital, Not Geriatric Specialty

Service lines, staffing, and marketing should span all age groups equally. Young Adult dominance (21.9%) is a long-term acquisition opportunity — engaged early, retained long-term. Previous geriatric-specialization strategy recommendations must be revisited.

Blood Type Distribution — All 8 Types at ~12.5% Each

All eight blood types are equally distributed across 351,765 patients — each at approximately 12.3%–12.6%, with only 1,116 patients separating the largest (B–) from the smallest (O+).

  • No clinical supply concentration risk by blood type
  • Gender equally balanced within every blood type group
  • Supports standardised blood bank inventory across all types
Source: Exercise 1 — Blood Type Filtering | Exercise 2 — Gender Analysis
Patient Distribution by Age Group — Five Groups Nearly Equal, Seniors Are the Smallest Cohort

Young Adults lead at 76,993 (21.9%), with Middle Age (50–64) as the smallest group at 66,999 (19.0%). Directly corrects the previous 85.5% elderly claim and reframes the hospital as a balanced, all-age general service facility. All strategic decisions built on geriatric dominance must be updated.

Source: Exercise 3 — Age Distribution

Allergy Risk & Patient Safety:64.5% Severe Burden — Uninsured Patients, Highest Clinical Risk
64.5% severe allergy burden — uninsured patients carry the highest clinical risk

Allergy severity is the most immediate patient safety variable in the dataset. With 64.5% of documented allergies classified as Severe, every clinical encounter carries compounded risk if allergy records are not verified at the point of prescribing. The intersection of allergy burden with insurance status creates a dual-exposure cohort — uninsured patients with severe allergies who are both the highest clinical risk and the lowest revenue-generating segment.

Patient Retention & Engagement:Strong Loyalty, Failing Pipeline — 78% Acquisition Collapse
Outstanding readmission performance — but acquisition collapsed 78% and 56% never return after visit 1

The retention story is one of two simultaneous realities. For patients who stay, the organisation delivers exceptional care — an 11.36% readmission rate placing it in the top 10–15% nationally. For patients who do not stay, the system is failing at the most critical moment: the first visit. More than half never return. Monthly new patient acquisition has fallen 78% over 12 months. The $303K average lifetime value of established patients makes every retained patient worth fighting for — and every lost first-visit patient a measurable revenue gap.

Outstanding readmission performance — treatment completion critically low at 13%

Care quality has two faces in this dataset. The readmission rate is a genuine organisational achievement — $324M in annual value relative to average performance, earned through clinical discipline and follow-up rigour. The 706-day maximum care gap and 100% URGENT classification of gap patients confirm that for a significant cohort, the system has lost contact entirely.

Treatment Completion Crisis: 10.3-Day Average Gap Between Treatment Events

The 10.3-day average between treatment events is not the core problem — it is a symptom. Patients who experience their first treatment gap are 3.9× less likely to complete their pathway. The critical intervention window is the 10-day period immediately following the first missed treatment event.

Treatment Continuity Crisis — 42% of Treatments Fail or Are Abandoned

Only 13% Completed, while 42% end in Failed (15%), Not Tolerated (15%), or Declined (12%). Partially Completed leads at 20%. Average 10.3 days between treatment events contributes to dropout.

Source: Exercise 32
Treatment Completion Triples by Step 3 — But Only 12% Overall Finish

Completion climbs from 9% at Step 1 → 11% Step 2 → 35% Step 3. Patients who persist are 3.9x more likely to complete. Critical intervention point is the Step 1 to Step 2 transition where the majority are permanently lost.

Source: Exercise 33
All 100 Patients Overdue for Care — Longest Gap 706 Days Without a Visit

100% of care gap patients URGENT, 100% carry active allergy documentation gaps. 23 patients overdue 550+ days, 22 in the 270–365 day range. Problem broadly distributed — reactivating even the most overdue quartile delivers revenue recovery and patient safety improvement.

Source: Exercise 35
Patient Journey:Risk Escalates with Time — 18 CRITICAL Patients in Established Tier
Established patients (180+ days) carry the highest CRITICAL and HIGH risk concentration

Patient risk does not stabilise with time in the system — it escalates. Established patients (180+ days) carry the highest concentration of CRITICAL and HIGH risk patients, with an average lifetime value of $303K. This pattern means that the patients with the greatest financial value to the organisation are simultaneously the patients with the most complex clinical needs. Risk management cannot be a one-time intake assessment — it requires continuous longitudinal monitoring calibrated to tenure.

88 Established Patients — 18 CRITICAL and 70 HIGH Risk Concentrated at Journey End

Established patients (180+ days) contain the highest concentration of CRITICAL (18) and HIGH (70) risk patients with avg LTV $303K. Risk escalates as a function of time in system — demands continuous longitudinal monitoring rather than one-time intake assessment.

Source: Exercise 36
Cross-Reference — Section E

Risk Scoring Technique Documented in Section E — Pages 12–13

The CRITICAL/HIGH risk classification applied throughout this page is produced by a 5-dimension composite scoring model built entirely in SQL using CASE WHEN logic across Allergy Burden, Utilisation, Treatment Adherence, Age Complexity, and Financial Exposure. The model is documented in full in Section E (Exercise 35) where it belongs — as a demonstration of analytical infrastructure capability.

  • Section E, Page 12: Risk score distribution — 8% CRITICAL, 92% HIGH, zero moderate or low in the 200-patient sample
  • Section E, Page 13: Care gap analysis — CRITICAL patients average 766 days since last visit; 100% of care gap patients URGENT

The key connection: both findings were only possible because of the composite scoring infrastructure. The patient journey pattern shown here is the business outcome — Section E provides the technical proof.

Implications of the Journey–Risk Pattern

  • Long-term patients accumulate clinical complexity — risk scores must be reviewed on 90-day cycles
  • Care coordinators should be assigned based on tenure + risk score, not just intake severity
  • $303K avg LTV of Established patients makes them the highest-value retention priority
  • 18 Established CRITICAL patients warrant dedicated case management immediately
